rationale: Health-code-driven consumable route with a proven branch model (Auto-Chlor), but pricing is MISSING, machine capex per placement delays payback, and Ecolab/Auto-Chlor/distributor bundles dominate. Realistic yr3-5 owner FCF ~$75-125k; ROIC diluted by placed-machine capital and restaurant closures.
red_flags: Ecolab segment margin is incumbent economics, not new-entrant

rationale: Published Easy Ice pricing (B) anchors ticket, but machine cost, service burden and term length are assumptions. Asset-heavy per account (~30-60% return on machine capital), refrigeration techs scarce, national roll-up competitor actively consolidating. Better as add-on to a dish/chemical route than standalone.
red_flags: dealer restrictions on rental programs unverified

rationale: Low-ticket ($60-120/mo) commodity rental against Culligan, Primo, Cintas; per-unit returns fine but absolute profit small and sales cost per unit high. Office occupancy decline hurts; warehouse niche is plausible but unproven. Best as cross-sell SKU.

Cintas segment (A) proves demand and high incumbent margins; independent van distributors are a known model. Very low capital, established route-rep role, consumable recurring demand. Independent wholesale costs and per-site spend are MISSING; switching away from bundled Cintas contracts is the key unproven step.
red_flags: incumbent 57.7% GM not transferable to sub-scale buyer

rationale: Cheap to start but tiny per-unit tickets, all economics E, Cintas/Rentokil/janitorial bundling compete. Viable only as an extra SKU on a denser multi-service route; standalone ceiling low. Sanitary-waste classification unresolved.
Plant-scale incumbents (Cintas+UniFirst) with route density; outsourced laundering to a would-be competitor's plant squeezes margin and supply is unverified. Record itself caps at ~$10k/mo. Poor fit.

Discretionary marketing spend, no spending evidence retrieved, ScentAir/Prolitec plus cheap direct-to-business diffusers online. High gross margin claim is unsupported; churn in downturns likely. Low ceiling.

Office-centric discretionary spend weakened post-2020; holiday decor is a decent door-opener but seasonal. Pricing and margins are all E; Ambius and many local firms compete. Pesticide licensing avoidable or obtainable.

Very accessible buyers, same-visit sales, near-zero capital and paid-at-service cash, Gasket Guy shows the model (D). But tickets are small and per-metro volume limited; easily copied. Strong as bundle on a kitchen route, weak standalone.

Tiny capital and dense Chicago bar base, but willingness to pay unproven, many bars self-clean or rely on distributors, US beer volume declining, and Illinois tied-house treatment unresolved. Record itself caps near $10k/mo.

Labor-margin repair service with portfolio access via property managers; low capital. No pricing evidence; OEM parts access varies; profits scale only with technician headcount. Realistic base ~$50-90k.

Mandated recurring demand (NFPA 110/CMS) is real and growing, but code text, prices and spend were not retrieved; generator dealers hold PM contracts and bundle; institutional buyers mean credibility walls and net-30-60. Equipment $15-60k. Plausible niche, unproven.

Dense Chicago warehouse base and insurer/EHS drivers, but inspections are not legally mandated, standards text not retrieved, non-OEM repairs may need engineer sign-off, and rack dealers bundle inspections. Liability at height. CV damage tagging is a modest AI lever.

Best-supported growth path in packet: GPRS (D) grew from one rented scanner to 54+ metros and buys local firms. Frequent contractor demand, short cycles, referrals, no license; fits tech background. Day rates MISSING, liability for misses, construction-cyclical, GPRS price pressure.

Districts identifiable but relationship/procurement-driven with summer seasonality and net-30-60; ESSER funding cliff and OEM/insurance/student-repair programs compete. Repair volumes and budgets all E. Labor-margin business with modest ceiling.

Recurring HOA/business-park contracts, Chicago suburbs dense with retention ponds, acquisitive SOLitude provides exit/proxy (D). Exam-based aquatic applicator license (A) obtainable in months. Pricing MISSING, seasonal labor, fish-kill liability, NPDES unverified.
Liability-driven but voluntary inspections; public procurement friction, seasonality, small tickets, dealer competition. No pricing or spend evidence. Low ceiling.

Near-zero capital, repeatable per-property contracts, Valet Living since 1995 proves model (D). But per-unit pricing MISSING, evening labor reliability is the core risk, Chicago-area adoption lower than Sunbelt, and resident fee pass-through faces junk-fee/fire-code scrutiny. Easily copied.
red_flags: fire-code limits on hallway bags not addressed

rationale: Essential demand but consolidated nationals, 5-10-year contracts lock larger buildings, small buildings have low vend volume, and machine capital returns only ~25-40%. Long payback, weak cash.

Good incumbent data (WillScot A): $286/mo rates but utilization fell to ~51.5%. At <=$100k a new entrant fields ~20-30 containers; meaningful FCF requires debt-financed fleet growth into a construction downturn. Long-lived assets, low ROIC (~20-35%).

Documented shortage (FHWA, C) and prepaid monthly rent, near-absentee ops. But zoning/special-use approval and leasable land are the gate; industrial outdoor storage competes for land at high rents; spot rates and lease costs MISSING; improvements plus lease commitment may exceed $100k before revenue.

Permit-driven demand with infrastructure tailwinds, but fleet capex, net-45-60 receivables, incumbents tied to big contractors (often DBE-certified), struck-by safety risk and insurance costs. No spend or rate evidence.

Thin-margin labor contracting, few DC decision makers with incumbent contracts and 6-18-month cycles, payroll float, injury and labor-law exposure (possible Day and Temporary Labor Services Act). No evidence at all.
Dominant incumbent (AIR-serv, 70k+ sites) with chains locked; independents only; low per-machine income, vend counts MISSING. Record caps at ~$10k/mo.

Mandated recurring demand with a documented ~$20 calibration fee (B), but the provider controls client routing, volume per territory is unknown, and the record caps near $10k/mo. A side line for an existing auto bay, not a standalone company.

Strong incumbent evidence (Accel A) shows the opposite of an opening: $150-500k before revenue, 18-month licensing with heavy background disclosure, locations already contracted, Accel pays ~$0.84M/location. Founder age/background requirements unknown. Not viable de novo.
Declining cash use, scale-dominated processing, vault cash tied up, theft risk, no wedge. Record caps at ~$10k/mo.

Growing, recession-resistant demand (CANA, C) with sticky weekly clinic relationships and a credible own-retort upgrade path. But all pricing is E, early phase depends on a competitor's crematory, retort/air-permit phase needs ~$150-300k, and corporate vet consolidators centralize vendors. Illinois pet crematory rules MISSING.

Illinois Funeral Directors Code defines removal as funeral directing; unlicensed staff historically could assist only under a licensed FD (2004 text: FD accompanies calls) [quick check, current text unverified]. Requires licensed FD employee/partner, which may destroy unit economics. Demand durable; rates MISSING.
red_flags: core legality left MISSING by record

rationale: Strong demographic tailwind (cremation 62.8%->69.1%, C) and prepaid cases; buyers search at time of need. Needs employed licensed FD and establishment license; Chicago direct-cremation market crowded with low-price brands and high CPCs. Case pricing, trade crematory fees and CAC all E.
Deposits aid cash, but structural decline as cremation share rises (A), funeral homes and cemeteries capture sales/installs, dealer margins unknown. Low-moderate ceiling.

Acyclical emergency demand with $2-15k tickets and referral networks (police, coroners, property managers); Aftermath and franchise systems show viability (D). No Illinois practitioner license found (2021 bill only introduced). Ad competition from franchises, insurer receivables 30-90 days, technician burnout.
Prepaid, near-zero capital, but A-level evidence shows the legalization market shrinking as countries join the Apostille Convention; crowded online. Record caps at ~$10k/mo.

Low-capex fiber-laser shop with national e-commerce reach and repeat OEM orders; configurator/instant-quote is a modest AI lever. But nameplate spend and pricing MISSING, fragmented competitors already sell online, OEM qualification slows wins. Manufacturing-cyclical.

Real export-compliance need and Chicago machinery base, but 30-45% GM labor/lumber business, large logistics firms hold ~89% of receipts, export cycles and tariffs, ISPM-15 certification path MISSING.
Inventory-heavy, one sales season per year, gatekept by band directors loyal to incumbent dealers, defaults and rent-to-own disclosure rules. Capital up to $100k with 24-month profitability.
No spending evidence; tiny niche with low ceiling (record ~$10k/mo). Cheap and easy to start but easily copied and capped.
